• Check every odd digit in turn: position 4 (=9): previous position 3 = 6 (even) → fails.

 

• Position 5 (=9): previous position 4 = 9 (odd) ✓; next position 6 = 4 (even) ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Position 9 (=7): previous position 8 = 1 (odd) ✓; next position 10 = 5 (odd) → fails.

 

• Position 10 (=5): previous position 9 = 7 (odd) ✓; next position 11 = 6 (even) ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Checking the remaining odd digits (positions 2, 8, 13, 20, 21, 22) similarly, none satisfy both conditions.

 

• Total qualifying digits = position 5 and position 10 = Two.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Write the series with position numbers above each digit, then scan left to right marking only odd digits; for each, glance one position left and one position right — this systematic scan avoids missing or double-counting any digit.

 

NOTE

 

• The very first and last digits of the series can never qualify for a 'preceded by/followed by' condition, since they lack a digit on one side.

question:
Read the given statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s) from the statements.

Statements:

Some nut are bolt.

Some bolt are rivet.

Conclusions:

(I) Some nut are rivet.

(II) All rivet are bolt.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option A i.e. Neither conclusion (I) nor (II) follows.

 

GIVEN

 

• Statements: Some nut are bolt (I-type/particular affirmative). Some bolt are rivet (I-type/particular affirmative).

 

SOLUTION

 

• Both statements are particular (I-type) propositions. A basic rule of syllogism: two particular premises never yield a valid conclusion.

 

• Conclusion (I), 'Some nut are rivet', would require a common (middle) term to definitely link nut and rivet through bolt, but since both premises are only 'some', the overlapping nut-bolt group and bolt-rivet group may not actually overlap with each other — so it does not necessarily follow.

 

• Conclusion (II), 'All rivet are bolt', is a universal statement that clearly cannot be derived from two 'some' (particular) statements — it does not follow.

 

• Since neither conclusion is guaranteed to be true in every possible Venn diagram consistent with the statements, neither follows.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option A.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Golden rule of syllogism: 'Some' + 'Some' = No valid conclusion. Whenever both premises are particular (I-type) statements, immediately mark 'neither conclusion follows' without further Venn diagram analysis (unless there's a possibility-type conclusion being tested).

 

NOTE

 

• Draw at least two different valid Venn diagrams for the given statements to double check — if a conclusion is false in even one valid diagram, it does not 'follow'.

question:
Seven boxes A, B, C, D, E, F and G are kept one over the other but not necessarily in the same order.

Only three boxes are kept below D. Only two boxes are kept between D and E. Only C is kept immediately above A. F is kept at some place below B and at some place above G.

How many boxes are kept below G?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. 1.

 

GIVEN

 

• 7 boxes A–G stacked in positions 1 (topmost) to 7 (bottommost).

 

SOLUTION

 

• 'Only three boxes are kept below D' ⟹ D is at position 4 (3 boxes below it, at positions 5, 6, 7).

 

• 'Only two boxes are kept between D and E' ⟹ |pos(D) − pos(E)| = 3 ⟹ E = 1 or E = 7.

 

• Testing E = 7: remaining positions {1,2,3,5,6} are left for A, B, C, F, G.

 

• 'Only C is kept immediately above A' ⟹ C's position = A's position − 1 (a consecutive pair). Testing the pair (1,2): C=1, A=2.

 

• Remaining positions {3,5,6} go to B, F, G. 'F is below B and above G' ⟹ pos(B) < pos(F) < pos(G): B=3, F=5, G=6 satisfies this (3<5<6).

 

• Final order (top to bottom): C(1), A(2), B(3), D(4), F(5), G(6), E(7).

 

• Boxes below G (position 6): only position 7 (E) = 1 box.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• In linear/vertical arrangement puzzles, fix the box with the most specific numeric clue first (here, D at position 4, from 'only three below D'), then test the two possible positions for the next-most-constrained box (E) to see which one allows all remaining clues to be satisfied consistently.

 

NOTE

 

• 'X is kept immediately above Y' means X's position number is exactly one less than Y's (assuming position 1 = top), so their positions must be consecutive.

question: In a certain code language, 'MORE' is coded as '1637' and 'DEMO' is coded as '4176'. What is the code for 'D' in the given code language?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. 4.

 

GIVEN

 

• MORE → 1637; DEMO → 4176.

 

SOLUTION

 

• MORE and DEMO share three common letters: M, O, E; only R is unique to MORE and only D is unique to DEMO.

 

• Digits used in MORE's code = {1, 6, 3, 7}. Digits used in DEMO's code = {4, 1, 7, 6}.

 

• The digit for R (unique to MORE) must be the one in MORE's set that does NOT appear in DEMO's set: that digit is 3 (since 1, 6, 7 are common to both sets). So R = 3, and the remaining digits {1, 6, 7} belong to M, O, E.

 

• Similarly, the digit for D (unique to DEMO) must be the one in DEMO's set that does NOT appear in {1, 6, 7} (the digits for M, O, E): that digit is 4.

 

• So D is coded as 4.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• When two coded words share several letters, find the digit(s) that appear in ONE code but NOT the other — that 'leftover' digit must belong to the one letter that is unique to that word. This elimination method avoids needing to resolve the exact code of every shared letter.

 

NOTE

 

• This puzzle cannot always be solved by simply reading off the digit at the letter's position in the word — the digits are not always assigned in simple left-to-right order, so the elimination method (via unique letters) is the reliable approach.

question: Mohini starts from Point A and drives 13 km towards south. She then takes a right turn, drives 7 km, turns right and drives 7 km. She then takes a right turn and drives 3 km. She takes a final left turn, drives 6 km and stops at Point P. How far (shortest distance) and towards which direction should she drive in order to reach Point A again? (Note: All turns are 90° turns only unless specified.)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option A i.e. 4 km towards east.

 

GIVEN

 

• Mohini: starts at A, drives 13 km south, right turn + 7 km, right turn + 7 km, right turn + 3 km, LEFT turn + 6 km, stops at P.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Start facing south, drive 13 km south. Turn right ⟹ now facing west, drive 7 km west.

 

• Turn right ⟹ now facing north, drive 7 km north.

 

• Turn right ⟹ now facing east, drive 3 km east.

 

• Turn LEFT ⟹ now facing north, drive 6 km north.

 

• Net North-South displacement: −13 (south) + 7 (north) + 6 (north) = −13 + 13 = 0 (back to the original latitude).

 

• Net East-West displacement: −7 (west) + 3 (east) = −4 (4 km west of A), so P is 4 km west of A.

 

• To return from P to A, she must travel 4 km towards east.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option A.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Track North-South and East-West displacements as two separate running totals as you go through each leg — the final direction back to start is simply the reverse of the net resultant direction.

 

NOTE

 

• Carefully distinguish 'right turn' from the one 'left turn' in the question — missing that single left turn (which reverses the usual right-turn rotation) is the most common error in this type of problem.

question: GKPY is related to JFST in a certain way based on the English alphabetical order. In the same way, SQBE is related to VLEZ. To which of the following options is BBKP related, following the same logic?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. EWNK.

 

GIVEN

 

• GKPY : JFST :: SQBE : VLEZ :: BBKP : ?

 

SOLUTION

 

• Check the pattern letter by letter for GKPY → JFST: G(7)→J(10): +3; K(11)→F(6): −5; P(16)→S(19): +3; Y(25)→T(20): −5. The pattern alternates +3, −5, +3, −5 across the four letters.

 

• Verify with SQBE → VLEZ: S(19)→V(22): +3 ✓; Q(17)→L(12): −5 ✓; B(2)→E(5): +3 ✓; E(5)→Z: 5−5=0, which wraps to 26=Z ✓ (cyclic).

 

• Apply the same +3, −5, +3, −5 pattern to BBKP: B(2)+3=5=E; B(2)−5=−3→(mod 26)=23=W; K(11)+3=14=N; P(16)−5=11=K.

 

• Result = EWNK.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Always verify a suspected alternating pattern (like +3, −5, +3, −5) using BOTH given example pairs before applying it — this confirms the rule and also reveals whether cyclic wraparound (mod 26) is needed.

 

NOTE

 

• When a computed position goes below 1 or above 26, wrap around using mod 26 (e.g., a result of 0 represents Z, and a result of −3 becomes 26−3=23).

question:
What should come in place of the question mark (?) in the given series?

55 14 58 14 61 14 ?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. 64.

 

GIVEN

 

• Series: 55, 14, 58, 14, 61, 14, ?

 

SOLUTION

 

• This is a combined series: the digits at odd positions (1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th) form one series, and the digits at even positions (2nd, 4th, 6th) form another (constant) series.

 

• Odd positions: 55, 58, 61, ? — the pattern increases by +3 each time: 55→58→61→64.

 

• Even positions: 14, 14, 14 — a constant value inserted between each term of the main series.

 

• Since position 7 (the '?') is an odd position, it follows the +3 pattern: 61 + 3 = 64.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• When a series alternates between a changing sequence and a repeated constant, ignore the constant term and focus only on the changing sub-sequence at the relevant (odd or even) positions.

 

NOTE

 

• Don't be misled by the repeated '14' into thinking the entire series is constant — always separate interleaved series into their own independent tracks first.

question: Based on the English alphabetical order, three of the following four letter-cluster pairs are alike in a certain way and thus form a group. Which is the letter-cluster pair that DOES NOT belong to that group? (Note: The odd one out is not based on the number of consonants/vowels or their position in the letter-cluster.)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. NR – PT.

 

GIVEN

 

• Pairs: MQ–JS, NR–PT, UY–RA, RV–OX.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Check the letter-shift pattern within each pair (1st letter shift, 2nd letter shift):

 

• MQ→JS: M(13)→J(10) = −3; Q(17)→S(19) = +2.

 

• NR→PT: N(14)→P(16) = +2; R(18)→T(20) = +2.

 

• UY→RA: U(21)→R(18) = −3; Y(25)→A(1, cyclic) = +2 (25+2=27≡1).

 

• RV→OX: R(18)→O(15) = −3; V(22)→X(24) = +2.

 

• Three pairs (MQ-JS, UY-RA, RV-OX) all follow the same pattern: first letter −3, second letter +2. Only NR–PT follows a different pattern (+2, +2), making it the odd one out.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• For 'odd one out' letter-pair questions, compute the shift for BOTH letters in every option as a pair of numbers (e.g., '−3, +2') — the three that share an identical number-pair form the group, and the mismatched one is the answer.

 

NOTE

 

• Watch for cyclic wraparound (like Y+2 → A) when checking the second-letter shift — don't dismiss a pattern just because it seems to 'go past Z'.

question:
In a certain code language,

'A ? B' means 'A is the daughter of B',

'A = B' means 'A is the son of B',

'A @ B' means 'A is the father of B' and

'A √ B' means 'A is the sister of B'.

How is C related to L if 'C ? D @ E = F √ L'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option D i.e. Sister's daughter.

 

GIVEN

 

• ? = daughter of, = = son of, @ = father of, √ = sister of.

 

• Expression: C ? D @ E = F √ L.

 

SOLUTION

 

• 'C ? D': C is the daughter of D. 'D @ E': D is the father of E. So C and E are D's children (C, a daughter, is E's sister).

 

• 'E = F': E is the son of F. Since D is already E's father, F must be E's other parent, i.e. F is E's mother — and, by the standard nuclear-family assumption, also C's mother.

 

• 'F √ L': F is the sister of L, so L is F's sibling.

 

• Since C's mother is F, and L is F's sibling, C is L's sister's daughter (i.e., C is the daughter of L's sister F) — describing C's relation to L.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option D.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• In family-relation coded puzzles, redraw the family tree step by step as you decode each symbol, and always double-check which direction the final question asks ("C related to L" is answered as "C is L's ___", not the reverse).

 

NOTE

 

• Be careful with the direction of relations like 'A is sister of B' — it confirms A's gender (female) but the puzzle's context (here, the standard nuclear-family sharing of both parents) is what links C into L's family tree as a niece.

question:
Read the given statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s) from the statements.

Statements: All forks are kettles. Some forks are cups.

Conclusion (I): Some kettles are cups.

Conclusion (II): All cups are forks.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option D i.e. Only conclusion (I) follows.

 

GIVEN

 

• Statements: All forks are kettles (A-type/universal affirmative). Some forks are cups (I-type/particular affirmative).

 

SOLUTION

 

• Since All forks are kettles and Some forks are cups, the forks that are cups (from the second statement) are, by the first statement, definitely also kettles.

 

• This means: Some cups are kettles, which is logically the same as (by simple conversion) Some kettles are cups — so Conclusion (I) follows.

 

• Conclusion (II), 'All cups are forks', is a universal statement — but we only know 'SOME forks are cups', not that every cup is a fork; there could be other cups that have nothing to do with forks. So Conclusion (II) does not follow.

 

• Hence, only Conclusion (I) is valid.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option D.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Rule: 'All A are B' + 'Some A are C' → 'Some B are C' (and its converse 'Some C are B') always validly follows — this is a standard, frequently-tested valid syllogism combination.

 

NOTE

 

• A particular (Some) statement can never be 'strengthened' into a universal (All) conclusion — this is a common trap conclusion to watch for.

question: In a row of 32 people facing north, Anita is 8th from the left end. If Savita sits 9th to the right of Anita, then what is Savita's position from the right end of the row?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option D i.e. 16th.

 

GIVEN

 

• Row of 32 people; Anita is 8th from the left end; Savita sits 9th to the right of Anita.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Anita's position from the left = 8.

 

• Savita's position from the left = Anita's position + 9 = 8 + 9 = 17.

 

• Position from the right end = (Total people) − (position from left) + 1 = 32 − 17 + 1 = 16.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option D.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Formula: Position from right = (Total) − (Position from left) + 1. Always use this conversion formula directly rather than trying to count positions manually.

 

NOTE

 

• '9th to the right of Anita' means ADD 9 to Anita's position (not count Anita as the 1st of those 9); this is a common point of confusion.

question:
What should come in place of the question mark (?) in the given series?

66 81 98 117 138 ?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option A i.e. 161.

 

GIVEN

 

• Series: 66, 81, 98, 117, 138, ?

 

SOLUTION

 

• Find consecutive differences: 81−66=15, 98−81=17, 117−98=19, 138−117=21.

 

• The differences form their own arithmetic pattern: 15, 17, 19, 21 — increasing by 2 each time.

 

• Next difference = 21 + 2 = 23. So the next term = 138 + 23 = 161.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option A.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• When first differences themselves form a simple arithmetic progression (increasing by a constant), the series is essentially quadratic — just extend the difference pattern by one more step and add it to the last term.

 

NOTE

 

• Always write out the differences explicitly in a row below the series — visually spotting the +2 pattern in the differences is much easier than trying to guess the rule mentally.

question: Saurav starts from Point A and drives 9 km towards the east. He then takes a right turn, drives 6 km, turns right and drives 11 km. He then takes a right turn and drives 11 km. He takes a final right turn, drives 2 km and stops at Point P. How far (shortest distance) and towards which direction should he drive in order to reach Point A again? (All turns are 90 degrees turns only, unless specified.)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. 5 km to the south.

 

GIVEN

 

• Saurav: starts at A, drives 9 km east, then 4 consecutive RIGHT turns with legs of 6 km, 11 km, 11 km, 2 km, stops at P.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Start facing east, drive 9 km east. Right turn ⟹ facing south, drive 6 km south.

 

• Right turn ⟹ facing west, drive 11 km west. Right turn ⟹ facing north, drive 11 km north.

 

• Right turn ⟹ facing east, drive 2 km east.

 

• Net East-West displacement: +9 (east) − 11 (west) + 2 (east) = 0.

 

• Net North-South displacement: −6 (south) + 11 (north) = +5 (5 km north of A), so P is 5 km north of A.

 

• To return from P to A, Saurav must travel 5 km towards south.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• With four consecutive RIGHT turns (all 90°), the direction cycles East→South→West→North→East; track net East-West and net North-South displacement separately, then the return direction is simply the opposite of the resultant.

 

NOTE

 

• Since all four turns here are in the same (right) direction, the four legs of travel simply rotate through all four compass directions once each — a quick way to set up the displacement equations.

question: M, N, O, P, W, X and Y are sitting around a circular table facing the centre of the table. O sits to the immediate right of P. Only three people sit between O and Y when counted from the left of O. Only three people sit between P and N when counted from the left of P. W sits to the immediate right of M. How many people sit between X and M when counted from the left of M?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option D i.e. Two.

 

GIVEN

 

• 7 people M, N, O, P, W, X, Y sit around a circular table, facing the centre.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Since all are facing the centre, moving clockwise around the table corresponds to moving to each person's left (a standard convention for centre-facing circular arrangements).

 

• Fix O at position 0. 'O sits to the immediate right of P' ⟹ P is O's immediate right neighbour ⟹ P is one step counter-clockwise from O ⟹ P = position 6 (i.e. −1 mod 7).

 

• 'Only three people between O and Y, counted from the left of O' ⟹ Y is 4 steps clockwise from O ⟹ Y = position 4.

 

• 'Only three people between P and N, counted from the left of P' ⟹ N is 4 steps clockwise from P (position 6) ⟹ N = 6+4 = 10 mod 7 = position 3.

 

• Remaining positions {1, 2, 5} are left for M, W, X. 'W sits to the immediate right of M' ⟹ W is one step counter-clockwise from M ⟹ M = W + 1. Testing W=1, M=2 (since 1+1=2) works; then X = 5.

 

• Final positions: O=0, W=1, M=2, N=3, Y=4, X=5, P=6.

 

• 'People between X and M, counted from the left of M' means counting clockwise from M(2) to X(5): positions strictly between are 3 and 4 (N and Y) = Two people.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option D.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• For centre-facing circular arrangements, remember: clockwise movement = each person's LEFT side; counter-clockwise = each person's RIGHT side. Fixing this convention at the start prevents left-right confusion throughout the puzzle.

 

NOTE

 

• 'Only three people between X and Y, counted from the left of X' always means Y is exactly 4 positions clockwise from X (3 people occupy the seats strictly in between).

question: Based on the English alphabetical order, three of the following four letter-cluster pairs are alike in a certain way and thus form a group. Which is the letter-cluster pair that DOES NOT belong to that group? (Note: The odd one out is not based on the number of consonants/vowels or their position in the letter-cluster.)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option D i.e. MQ – PN.

 

GIVEN

 

• Pairs: FL–IJ, PJ–SH, LD–OB, MQ–PN.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Check the shift of each letter within a pair (1st letter shift, 2nd letter shift):

 

• FL→IJ: F(6)→I(9) = +3; L(12)→J(10) = −2.

 

• PJ→SH: P(16)→S(19) = +3; J(10)→H(8) = −2.

 

• LD→OB: L(12)→O(15) = +3; D(4)→B(2) = −2.

 

• MQ→PN: M(13)→P(16) = +3; Q(17)→N(14) = −3 (not −2).

 

• Three pairs (FL-IJ, PJ-SH, LD-OB) follow the pattern first letter +3, second letter −2. MQ–PN breaks the pattern with a −3 shift on the second letter, making it the odd one out.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option D.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Reduce each option to a pair of shift-numbers (e.g. '+3, −2') and simply spot which one differs from the other three — a quick, visual way to catch the odd one out without re-deriving the whole logic each time.

 

NOTE

 

• Always check the SECOND letter's shift too — many odd-one-out traps only break the pattern on the second letter, matching correctly on the first.

question: Five people, L, M, N, O and P, are sitting in a row facing north. N is sitting at the third position from the extreme right end of the row. M is not an immediate neighbour of N. P is sitting to the immediate left of N. P is sitting to the immediate right of O. Who is sitting between N and M?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. L.

 

GIVEN

 

• 5 people L, M, N, O, P in a row (positions 1–5 from left), facing north.

 

SOLUTION

 

• 'N is 3rd from the extreme right end' ⟹ N's position from left = 5 − 3 + 1 = 3.

 

• 'P sits immediately left of N' ⟹ P = position 2.

 

• 'P sits immediately right of O' ⟹ O = position 1.

 

• Remaining positions {4, 5} are left for L and M. 'M is not an immediate neighbour of N (position 3)' ⟹ M cannot be at position 4 (adjacent to N), so M = 5, and L = 4.

 

• Final order: O(1), P(2), N(3), L(4), M(5).

 

• Person sitting between N(3) and M(5) is at position 4 = L.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• After placing the directly-stated positions, use elimination for the negative clue ('is NOT an immediate neighbour of') on the remaining unplaced people — negative clues are best applied last, after most positions are already fixed.

 

NOTE

 

• 'Third from the right end' in a row of 5 always converts to position (5−3+1)=3 from the left — remember the formula: position from left = Total − position from right + 1.

question:
What should come in place of the question mark (?) in the given series based on the English alphabetical order?

NSE MRD LQC KPB ?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. JOA.

 

GIVEN

 

• Series: NSE, MRD, LQC, KPB, ?

 

SOLUTION

 

• Track each letter position across the series: 1st letters N(14), M(13), L(12), K(11) → decreasing by 1 each time → next = J(10).

 

• 2nd letters: S(19), R(18), Q(17), P(16) → decreasing by 1 each time → next = O(15).

 

• 3rd letters: E(5), D(4), C(3), B(2) → decreasing by 1 each time → next = A(1).

 

• Combined next cluster = JOA.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Whenever each letter cluster in a series is just 'one less' at every position than the previous cluster, the whole series is simply shifting back by 1 letter uniformly — extend this pattern directly without needing to separately verify each column once the pattern is clear from the first couple of steps.

 

NOTE

 

• Convert letters to alphabet numbers (A=1...Z=26) before checking for arithmetic patterns — this avoids errors from trying to subtract letters directly.

question:
Refer to the following number and symbol series and answer the question that follows. Counting to be done from left to right only. All numbers are single-digit numbers.

(Left) 3 & 6 © 3 6 © € % 6 & 4 9 5 4 % € £ $ % 9 1 (Right)

How many such numbers are there, each of which is immediately preceded by a symbol and also immediately followed by a symbol?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. 2.

 

GIVEN

 

• Series: 3 & 6 © 3 6 © € % 6 & 4 9 5 4 % € £ $ % 9 1 (22 terms, positions 1–22).

 

SOLUTION

 

• Position each term: 1:3, 2:&, 3:6, 4:©, 5:3, 6:6, 7:©, 8:€, 9:%, 10:6, 11:&, 12:4, 13:9, 14:5, 15:4, 16:%, 17:€, 18:£, 19:$, 20:%, 21:9, 22:1.

 

• We need a NUMBER at position i such that position (i−1) is a symbol AND position (i+1) is a symbol.

 

• Position 3 (=6): previous (position 2)=& (symbol) ✓; next (position 4)=© (symbol) ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Position 10 (=6): previous (position 9)=% (symbol) ✓; next (position 11)=& (symbol) ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Checking the remaining number positions (1, 5, 6, 12, 13, 14, 15, 21, 22) similarly, none of them have symbols on BOTH sides.

 

• Total qualifying numbers = 2 (positions 3 and 10).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Number the series positions first, then scan only the NUMBER positions and check one step left and one step right at each — a systematic left-to-right scan avoids missing any qualifying term in a long mixed series.

 

NOTE

 

• The first and last positions of the series can never qualify, since they don't have a term on both sides.

question:
Refer to the following number series and answer the question that follows (all numbers are single-digit numbers only). Counting to be done from left to right only.

(Left) 1 6 4 5 6 6 4 7 4 4 2 4 7 4 3 1 9 2 4 3 6 9 7 8 2 7 1 (Right)

How many such even numbers are there, each of which is immediately preceded by an odd number and also immediately followed by an even number?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. Five.

 

GIVEN

 

• Series: 1 6 4 5 6 6 4 7 4 4 2 4 7 4 3 1 9 2 4 3 6 9 7 8 2 7 1 (27 terms, positions 1–27).

 

SOLUTION

 

• We need an EVEN number at position i such that: digit(i−1) is odd AND digit(i+1) is even.

 

• Position 2 (=6): previous (=1) odd ✓; next (position 3=4) even ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Position 5 (=6): previous (position 4=5) odd ✓; next (position 6=6) even ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Position 9 (=4): previous (position 8=7) odd ✓; next (position 10=4) even ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Position 18 (=2): previous (position 17=9) odd ✓; next (position 19=4) even ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Position 24 (=8): previous (position 23=7) odd ✓; next (position 25=2) even ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Checking all other even positions similarly, no more qualify. Total = Five (positions 2, 5, 9, 18, 24).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Mark all EVEN numbers in the series first with a highlight/underline, then check only those positions for the odd-before, even-after condition — this narrows the search space considerably in a long series.

question: In a certain code language, 'TOUR' is coded as '4139' and 'BRUT' is coded as '4318'. What is the code for 'B' in the given code language?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. 8.

 

GIVEN

 

• TOUR → 4139; BRUT → 4318.

 

SOLUTION

 

• TOUR and BRUT share three common letters: T, U, R; only O is unique to TOUR and only B is unique to BRUT.

 

• Digits in TOUR's code = {4, 1, 3, 9}. Digits in BRUT's code = {4, 3, 1, 8}.

 

• The digit for O (unique to TOUR) must be the one in TOUR's set NOT present in BRUT's set: that is 9 (since 4, 1, 3 are common to both). So O = 9, and the remaining digits {4, 1, 3} belong to T, U, R.

 

• The digit for B (unique to BRUT) must be the one in BRUT's set NOT present in {4, 1, 3}: that is 8.

 

• So B is coded as 8.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• When two coded words overlap in most of their letters, find the digit set difference between the two codes — the digit unique to each word's code-set corresponds to the one letter unique to that word. This elimination trick avoids needing to fully decode every shared letter.

 

NOTE

 

• Do not assume the code digits are assigned strictly in the order the letters appear in the word — as this question shows, a simple position-by-position reading can give the wrong answer; use the common-letter elimination method instead.

question:
If 'A' stands for '÷', 'B' stands for '×', 'C' stands for '+' and 'D' stands for '−', then what will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following equation?

6 B 44 A 3 D 21 C 44 = ?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. 111.

 

GIVEN

 

• A = ÷, B = ×, C = +, D = −.

 

• Expression: 6 B 44 A 3 D 21 C 44 = ?

 

SOLUTION

 

• Substitute the meanings: 6 × 44 ÷ 3 − 21 + 44 = ?

 

• Apply BODMAS: 6 × 44 = 264. 264 ÷ 3 = 88.

 

• Now: 88 − 21 + 44 = 67 + 44 = 111.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Substitute all letter-operators with their actual symbols in one clean pass first, then solve strictly by BODMAS (multiplication/division before addition/subtraction, left to right within the same priority level).

 

NOTE

 

• Re-check the letter-to-symbol key carefully before starting — since A, B, C, D here map to ÷, ×, +, − respectively (not in the more 'expected' alphabetical order of +,−,×,÷), it's easy to make a substitution error.

question:
Refer to the following series and answer the question that follows. Counting to be done from left to right only. (All numbers are single-digit numbers only).

(Left) 7 9 1 8 4 2 5 6 3 8 7 1 9 (Right)

How many odd numbers are there (from left to right) which are immediately followed by even numbers?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. Three.

 

GIVEN

 

• Series: 7 9 1 8 4 2 5 6 3 8 7 1 9 (13 terms, positions 1–13).

 

SOLUTION

 

• Check every odd digit and see whether the digit immediately after it is even:

 

• Position 1 (=7): next (position 2=9) odd → fails.

 

• Position 2 (=9): next (position 3=1) odd → fails.

 

• Position 3 (=1): next (position 4=8) even ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Position 7 (=5): next (position 8=6) even ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Position 9 (=3): next (position 10=8) even ✓ → qualifies.

 

• Position 11 (=7): next (position 12=1) odd → fails. Position 12 (=1): next (position 13=9) odd → fails. Position 13 (=9): last term, no next term.

 

• Total qualifying odd numbers = Three (positions 3, 7, 9).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Underline every odd number in the series first, then simply check the very next digit for each — a quick visual scan for 'odd, then even' pairs.

 

NOTE

 

• The last digit of the series can never qualify, since it has no digit following it.

question:

(Note: Operations should be performed on the whole numbers, without breaking down the numbers into their constituent digits. E.g. 13 — Operations on 13 such as adding/subtracting/multiplying to 13 can be performed. Breaking down 13 into 1 and 3 and then performing mathematical operations on 1 and 3 is not allowed.)

solution_text:

GIVEN

 

• Related sets: (50, 1200, 12) and (4, 120, 15).

 

SOLUTION

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

question: What major international goal does the High Seas Treaty aim to advance once in force?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Create marine protected areas.

(उच्च सागर संधि — समुद्री संरक्षित क्षेत्र)

 

• The treaty covers roughly two-thirds of the world's oceans, an area that was previously largely unregulated for conservation purposes, and seeks to conserve marine biodiversity, regulate environmental impact assessments for activities on the high seas, and ensure fair sharing of marine genetic resources.

 

• The treaty was adopted by UN member states in June 2023 and requires a minimum number of ratifications to enter into force; India has been among the countries supporting the treaty's goals of ocean conservation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option B.

 

Additional Information

 

• The BBNJ Agreement is often described as a landmark instrument to help achieve the global '30x30' target — protecting 30% of the world's land and oceans by 2030 — agreed under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022).

 

• UNCLOS (1982), sometimes called the 'Constitution of the Oceans', is the overarching international framework governing all uses of the seas and oceans, including territorial waters, the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), and the high seas.

 

• India ratified UNCLOS in 1995 and has consistently supported multilateral efforts toward sustainable ocean governance.

 

NOTE

 

• Restrict commercial shipping lanes (Option A): Not the treaty's focus — it deals with biodiversity conservation, not shipping regulation.

 

• Establish a global fisheries quota (Option C): Fisheries management is handled by separate bodies/agreements (like Regional Fisheries Management Organisations), not the primary aim of this treaty.

 

• Ban deep-sea mining (Option D): Deep-sea mining is regulated separately by the International Seabed Authority (ISA); the High Seas Treaty does not impose an outright ban on it.

question: In the 56th meeting of Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) held from 4 to 6 August 2025, real GDP growth for Q1 2026-27 was projected at:
solution_text:
The correct answer is 6.6%.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the 56th meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), held from 4 to 6 August 2025, the Reserve Bank of India projected real GDP growth for Q1 of FY 2026-27 at 6.6%. (मौद्रिक नीति समिति — 56वीं बैठक, वास्तविक जीडीपी वृद्धि अनुमान)

 

• The MPC, headed by the RBI Governor, is a six-member committee responsible for determining the policy repo rate needed to maintain price stability while keeping in mind the objective of economic growth, meeting bi-monthly (six times a year).

 

• GDP growth projections are a key input for setting monetary policy, since the MPC must balance controlling inflation against supporting economic growth in the country.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option B.

 

Additional Information

 

• The MPC's primary mandate is to keep Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation within the target band of 4% (+/- 2%), i.e., between 2% and 6%, as mandated under the RBI Act, 1934 (amended in 2016).

 

• The MPC consists of three RBI members (including the Governor as Chairperson) and three external members appointed by the Government of India.

 

• Key monetary policy tools include the repo rate, reverse repo rate, Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR), and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR).

 

NOTE

 

• 6.3%, 6.5% and 6.8% (Options A, C, D) are plausible nearby figures, but the actual RBI projection announced for Q1 FY2026-27 in the 56th MPC meeting was 6.6%.

question: Which of the following institutes was chosen by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) in January 2025 to establish South India's first Infectious Disease Research and Diagnostic Laboratory (IRDL)?
option_1: Kamineni Academy of Medical Sciences And Research Centre, Hyderabad
option_3: Sri Ramachandra Medical College and Research Institute, Chennai
option_4: Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute (BMCRI)
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute (BMCRI).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option D.

 

Additional Information

• ICMR has a network of specialised institutes across India focused on different disease areas, such as the National Institute of Virology (Pune), known for its work on viral diseases.

 

• Strengthening regional diagnostic and research infrastructure (like this South India IRDL) is part of India's broader push toward decentralised public health preparedness.

 

NOTE

question: Which wildlife area has been recently recognised as India's 107th national park?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Similipal.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Similipal, located in Odisha, has been recently recognised as India's 107th national park. (सिमिलिपाल — भारत का 107वाँ राष्ट्रीय उद्यान)

 

• Similipal is well known for being part of the Similipal Tiger Reserve, one of India's important tiger reserves under Project Tiger, and is also renowned for its rich biodiversity, including a notable population of melanistic (black) tigers.

 

• The area is also recognised as a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, reflecting its ecological significance beyond just tiger conservation, encompassing a wide variety of flora and fauna typical of the Eastern Ghats region.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option D.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's national park system has grown steadily since the country's first national park, Jim Corbett National Park (Uttarakhand), established in 1936 (originally as Hailey National Park).

 

• National Parks in India are declared under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and offer a higher degree of legal protection than wildlife sanctuaries, generally prohibiting activities like grazing and private land rights within their boundaries.

 

• India's tiger reserves are managed under Project Tiger (launched 1973) with oversight from the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA).

 

NOTE

 

• Buxa (Option A): A tiger reserve in West Bengal, known for its rich biodiversity, but not the area referenced as the 107th national park here.

 

• Nagarhole (Option B): A national park and tiger reserve in Karnataka, already an established national park, not the newly recognised one.

 

• Palamau (Option C): A tiger reserve in Jharkhand, one of India's earliest Project Tiger reserves, but not the one referenced as the 107th national park.
